keyVerseText: For they covered the face of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened; and they did eat every herb of the land, and all the fruit of the trees which the hail had left: and there remained not any green thing in the trees, or in the herbs of the field, through all the land of Egypt.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb חָשַׁךְ (châshak) is a primitive root that primarily conveys the idea of darkness or the act of darkening. Its core sense involves the withholding or absence of light, whether naturally as in the onset of night or figuratively as concealment or obscurity. This root meaning enriches the common English gloss by emphasizing not only physical darkness but also the notion of hiding or obscuring, which can imply spiritual or moral concealment beyond mere visual dimness.
usageInScripture: Throughout its 18 occurrences, חָשַׁךְ is consistently used to describe physical darkness, such as the earth or celestial bodies becoming darkened, but also extends to figurative uses like hiding or obscuring. The top translations like "be darkened," "shall be darkened," and "hideth" illustrate this dual usage. This range reveals the word’s flexibility in describing both natural phenomena and metaphorical states of concealment or confusion, reflecting a broad semantic field centered on the concept of darkness in various forms.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding חָשַׁךְ deepens our grasp of biblical themes where darkness often symbolizes separation from God, judgment, or the obscuring of truth. The verb’s root meaning of causing darkness or hiding aligns with the biblical narrative of sin bringing spiritual darkness and alienation. Yet, in the Christian faith, this darkness is not final; Christ is the light that overcomes it. Recognizing the original sense of חָשַׁךְ reminds believers of the seriousness of spiritual blindness and the hope found in God’s revelation that dispels darkness.
keyVerseReflection: Exodus 10:15 describes a plague where darkness covered the entire land of Egypt, so that the earth was darkened and vegetation was consumed. The use of חָשַׁךְ here vividly conveys the overwhelming and inescapable nature of this darkness, emphasizing the total judgment upon Egypt. This darkness is not merely the absence of light but an active covering that signifies God’s sovereign power to bring judgment and effect change in history.
